title: Mahajanaka's swim
hookLine: a shipwrecked prince swims on with no shore in sight
tomorrow: can hard work actually feel good?

cards: A long rehab, a job hunt, a skill that isn't clicking yet: some efforts have no finish line you can see. You send the next application without knowing if anyone reads it.
In the Jataka, Prince Mahajanaka is sailing out to make his fortune when the ship breaks apart in open sea. The others panic.
He eats a full meal, rubs his body with oil, climbs the mast, leaps as far clear of the wreck as he can, and starts swimming. Tradition says he swims for seven days. No shore in sight.

teach.h: WHY SWIM WHERE NO SHORE SHOWS?
teach.b: Then a sea goddess, Manimekhala, notices him. In the story she asks the obvious question: why work so hard out here, where no shore can be seen? His answer is the lesson.

Someone who keeps striving, he says, can't be blamed; even if he goes down, he goes down having done what was his to do. She tells him his effort is useless in an ocean this size. He holds his ground.
And moved by it, she lifts him up and carries him to land. Notice the order. He doesn't swim because he can see the shore.
He swims, and then help arrives. Tradition remembers this tale as the Bodhisatta perfecting effort.

teach.h: HE ATE, OILED, CHOSE HIS JUMP.
teach.b: It sounds like tough-guy advice, but look at what he did first: he ate, he oiled his skin against the sea, he chose his moment to jump.
The Dhammapada has a line for him. In Max Müller's words: "By rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm."

how: The Mahajanaka Jataka is one of the last ten Jataka tales, which tradition ties to the ten perfections; it is retold in sermons and on temple walls in Theravada countries as the tale of effort.

o: a prince's daring escape from a palace by night
a sea goddess testing sailors with a riddle
effort that keeps going before the goal is in view

games.q: inside the swim — tap the pairs.
p: swims with no shore in sight
he eats and oils his skin

s: Mahajanaka swam because he could see land
no shore was in sight; that's why the goddess asks why he bothers.
in the story, he prepares before he jumps
he eats, oils his skin and chooses his moment.
swim anyway means thrash until you're exhausted
he paces it, after doing the sensible things first.

games.q: your cousin has sent out job application after job application and heard nothing. she's about to stop. what would Mahajanaka say?
o: keep sending, and fix one thing in each application as you go.
wait until a sure thing comes along before trying again.
send as many as possible today, fast, changing nothing.
games.why: he swam with no shore in sight, but he'd eaten, oiled his skin and picked his moment. swim anyway, sensibly.

practice: Name one thing you've been tempted to drop because you can't see the end of it. Name what's most likely to stop you this week, and decide your next small stroke for when it does. Hold that plan in mind while the sit runs.

wordCard.voice: Mahajanaka's swim: effort that keeps going without seeing the shore, after doing the sensible things first.

orig.note: Pali name of the prince in Jataka 539, whom tradition ties to the perfection of effort.

carryVoice: Something to keep: swim anyway, because the goddess came on the seventh day, not the first. Talk tomorrow.
